title: Get the Maximum Score
statement:
You get two strictly increasing integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2`. A path begins at index 0 of either array and reads that array's values from left to right until it runs past the last element.

- When the value just read occurs in **both** arrays, the path may jump to the position of that same value in the other array and carry on reading from there (it may also stay where it is).
- A shared value at a jump is counted only once.

The score of a path is the sum of the values it reads. Find the largest possible score over all paths and return it modulo `10^9 + 7` (take the maximum first, then the remainder).
constraints: nums1 and nums2 are strictly increasing
notes:
## Intuition

The values that appear in both arrays are the only places where a path can change sides, and every path passes through all of them. So they cut both arrays into matching segments: between two consecutive shared values, a path reads either the whole `nums1` segment or the whole `nums2` segment. The best path simply takes the larger segment sum each time. Trying every combination of jumps (the brute force) is exponential; one merge-style pass is enough.

## Approach

1. Walk both arrays with `i` and `j` like a merge, keeping `sum1` and `sum2`: the best scores of paths that are currently on `nums1` and on `nums2`.
2. If `nums1[i]` is the smaller value (or `nums2` is used up), add it to `sum1` and advance `i`.
3. If `nums2[j]` is smaller (or `nums1` is used up), add it to `sum2` and advance `j`.
4. Equal values are a shared value: a path can arrive from either side, so set both sums to `best = max(sum1, sum2) + value` and advance both pointers.
5. At the end return `max(sum1, sum2)` modulo `10^9 + 7`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums1 = [2,4,5,8,10]`, `nums2 = [4,6,8,9]`. Read `2`: `sum1 = 2`. Shared `4`: `best = max(2, 0) + 4 = 6`, both sums become 6. Read `5`: `sum1 = 11`. Read `6`: `sum2 = 12`. Shared `8`: `best = max(11, 12) + 8 = 20`. Read `9`: `sum2 = 29`. Read `10`: `sum1 = 30`. The answer is `max(30, 29) = 30`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + m): every element is visited once.
- Space: O(1): only two running sums and two pointers.

## Pitfalls

- Apply the modulo only at the very end. Reducing `sum1` and `sum2` while walking breaks the `max` comparison.
- In languages with 32-bit integers the sums need 64 bits: `10^5 * 10^7` overflows an `int`.
- Add a shared value once, not once per array.
- Do not stop when one array runs out; the rest of the other array still counts.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `i`, `j` | next unread index in `nums1` and `nums2` |
| `sum1`, `sum2` | best score of a path ending on `nums1` / `nums2` so far |
| `best` | best score up to and including a shared value |
| `MOD` | `10^9 + 7`, applied once at the end |

narration.3: i points at the next unread value of nums1...
narration.4: ...and j at the next unread value of nums2.
narration.5: Best score of a path that is currently reading nums1.
narration.6: Best score of a path that is currently reading nums2.
narration.8: Merge both arrays until every value has been read.
narration.9: nums1 has the smaller next value (or nums2 is exhausted), so only a nums1 path can read it.
narration.10: Add it to the nums1 path's score.
narration.12: nums2 has the smaller next value (or nums1 is exhausted).
narration.13: Add it to the nums2 path's score.
narration.15: Otherwise both pointers show the same value: a shared value where paths can switch.
narration.16: Whichever side was better so far can arrive here, then the shared value is added once.
narration.17: From here on a nums1 path may have come from either side...
narration.19: Move past the shared value in nums1...
narration.23: Take the better final side, and only now reduce it modulo 10^9 + 7.
